job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Ivan Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me, Ivan. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent: no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mornings I'm up early at my parents' place in Alder Cove, sharing the house with my grandmother too. I run a little routine: scan new roles, let an AI assistant draft my first pass of a cover letter, then I rewrite it so it sounds like me. Afternoons I do freelance bookkeeping for two small shops, a bakery and a bike repair place, which brings in a bit. I try to end the day by messing with some automation, since that's the part I enjoy.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you study and what did you do in your internships?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Accounting and finance, top of my year. One internship was in the finance team of a logistics company, Corvane Freight, where I reconciled shipping invoices. The other was at a small advisory firm that does accounts for restaurants. I built a spreadsheet script at the logistics place that cut a day's matching to an hour, and the manager mostly said thanks and nothing else, which stung a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, which we call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, it's a better spreadsheet, and that's it. I already use it every day, and it saves me about an hour. I'd tell people not to buy the hype, because hype is how people get sold things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my situation doesn't change much. I still have some student debt, a few weeks of savings, and no offer yet. The tools keep me productive, but it's the market that's slow, and a quiet AI world doesn't fix a quiet hiring market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going with freelancing and try to grow it from two clients to five, mostly small shops that can't afford an accountant. I'd apply for ten roles a week, and I'd keep building automations for the bakery and the bike shop as portfolio pieces. I'd also join an online group of young accountants, because most of my good leads come from people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty okay, a bit restless. I like making things work, so the freelance work gives me energy. The no-offer part still sits in my stomach every Sunday night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the freelance work brings in a bit. How much, and how steady is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's about four hundred a month, and it varies. The bakery pays on time, the bike shop sometimes forgets. That covers my phone and train pass, and I give my mum something for groceries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame for the slow job market, if anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Firms keep saying they can't find talent, while rejecting everyone without three years of experience. Mostly the companies that cut entry-level hiring to look lean, and the funds that reward them for it. It's a rigged ladder, and I want unions or regulators to say hiring graduates is part of running a business.

say: I'd say it's a **better spreadsheet** and people shouldn't buy the hype.
I'd say firms are shrinking **entry-level hiring** to look lean, which is a rigged ladder.
think: My situation barely changes, because the real issue is a **slow hiring market**.
I'd keep my edge by being the person who makes **tools work**.
do: Grow the freelance work from two clients to **five small shops**.
Apply for **ten roles** a week and show the automations as portfolio pieces.
Join an **online group** of young accountants, since leads come from people.
feel: **Restless** and fairly upbeat, with Sunday-night worry about no offer.
S0.quote: Firms keep saying they can't find talent, while rejecting everyone without three years of experience.
fieldNote: Ivan is energised by tools, so the quiet scenario hardly dents him; his worry is the **hiring market**.
He blames structural choices by firms and funds, which fits his progressive view.
Side income gives him a real, if modest, cushion.

steps.text: Grow the freelance bookkeeping from two clients to five
Send ten applications a week for accounting roles
Build two spreadsheet automations for the bakery as portfolio pieces

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's what I'm seeing already: invoice matching, categorising, first drafts. Companies will hire fewer juniors, and some won't hire any. I'd say that if you can steer the tools, you're fine, but most people haven't been shown how.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm better placed than most, but the entry-level pool is still shrinking. My friends who skip the tools are the ones I worry about. I'm also annoyed that the first jobs, where you learn, are going and nobody is replacing them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the freelance work harder, because small firms will love anyone who sets up their books once and keeps them tidy. I'd build a package: set up, automate, monthly check. I'd also look at the jobs that sit between finance and data, like analyst roles, where tools are part of the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and uneasy at once. I feel like a surfer when the wave arrives, and I'm not sure whether I'm riding it or underneath it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of your own work are you handing over to the tools already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Almost everything routine: matching, coding, drafting emails to clients, even first-pass tax checks. I read the output, fix mistakes and sign off. If I'd been told to do it by hand, I'd have been slower and probably made more errors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want regulators to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Make companies publish how many junior roles they've cut and require some notice before big layoffs. Tax the savings a bit to fund retraining. And keep a human accountable for anything that touches someone's money, so you can ask a real person.

say: I'd say juniors who can **steer the tools** will be fine, but most haven't been shown how.
I'd say companies should publish **how many junior roles** they cut.
think: I'm better placed than most, but the **entry-level pool** keeps shrinking.
I worry about friends who **skip the tools** and see no first rung.
do: Push the **freelance** work, packaging set-up, automation and a monthly check for small firms.
Look at **analyst roles** that sit between finance and data.
Teach two friends the tools in a **weekend session**.
feel: **Excited and uneasy**, like on a surfboard, unsure if I'm riding the wave.
S1.quote: I feel like a surfer when the wave arrives, and I'm not sure whether I'm riding it or underneath it.
fieldNote: Ivan's stance is **dual**: he rides the tools but still wants rules and notice from companies.
Strong concern for peers who avoid tools shows solidarity, not just self-interest.
Freelance package idea is concrete and shows initiative.

steps.text: Sell small shops a set-up, automation and monthly check package
Run a weekend tool session for two friends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to tax the gains and pay people a floor. Two years is no time at all, and I'd say that out loud. I'd also post what I'm doing so other graduates can copy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think most junior accounting jobs vanish, and mine would too if I had one. The only advantage I have is speed: I'm already living with the tools. But if everyone else catches up in six months, my edge fades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast: build a small agency, me plus tools, offering books and reporting to small firms at a price a person couldn't match. I'd keep expenses at the bare minimum, since I live at home, and put away every cent. I'd also help my parents sort their money, because nobody else will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, yeah. A mix of adrenaline and nausea. I'm good at adapting, but I can't adapt for everyone, and that's what bothers me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the next 24 months actually go for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first six months I'd spend building the agency and getting five clients. By month twelve I'd either have steady monthly income or I'd know it's not working and take whatever job pays. By month twenty-four, who knows, that's the honest answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think gets hurt worst?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People with no savings, no tool skills and nobody to ask. My uncle processes invoices at a call centre, and he gets the news the same day as everyone else, but with nowhere to go. I'd want the government to reach them first, not me.

say: I'd say this is the time to **tax the gains** and pay people a floor.
I'd post what I'm doing so other graduates can **copy it**.
think: Most junior accounting jobs **vanish**, and my only edge is speed with the tools.
If everyone else catches up in six months, my **edge** fades.
do: Build a small **agency**, me plus tools, with five small-firm clients in six months.
Keep expenses minimal and **save every cent**, since I live at home.
Help my **parents** sort their money and spot scams.
feel: **Anxious**, a mix of adrenaline and nausea, mostly for people with no time to adapt.
S2.quote: My uncle processes invoices at a call centre, and he gets the news the same day as everyone else, but with nowhere to go.
fieldNote: Ivan converts anxiety into action: an **agency plan** with a six-month test.
His sharpest worry is for others, such as his uncle, which fits his progressive view.
Honest that his tool advantage may be short-lived.

steps.text: Sign five small-firm clients for books and reporting within six months
Save every spare cent while living at home
Set up safe banking and scam checks for my parents
Back an income floor by signing petitions

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a real chance, and we should build the safety net now, not after. I'd say to employers: train juniors now, because you'll need people who can run the tools. I'd also say it to my local MP.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel good about my chances but bad about the system. I could get a first job, make myself valuable by building automation, and save hard. But I'd want to see how many of my friends make it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a job that lets me work on automation, even at a modest salary, and keep freelancing on the side. I'd also learn enough about data and compliance to be the person who checks the machine. And I'd put money into an index fund each month, since I expect to need more than one income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, a bit guilty. I'm in good shape, and some friends aren't. I'd keep thinking about how to bring them along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years buy you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to climb a rung. A first job, then a second one with more responsibility, before the main change arrives. I could also have a small business with real clients, which beats a CV line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay in accounting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe in a different shape. I like finance, but I like building more, so a hybrid role fits. I'd rather be the person who designs the checks than the one who does them by hand.

say: I'd say five years is a **real chance**, so build the safety net now.
I'd tell employers to **train juniors** now, because they'll need people who run the tools.
think: I feel good about my chances but **bad about the system**.
I'd want to see how many of my **friends** make it.
do: Take a job on **automation**, even at modest pay, and keep freelancing.
Learn enough **data and compliance** to be the person who checks the machine.
Put money into an **index fund** monthly, expecting to need more than one income.
feel: **Hopeful** but a little guilty, because I'm in better shape than some friends.
S3.quote: I'd rather be the person who designs the checks than the one who does them by hand.
fieldNote: Five years gives Ivan a **ladder** plan: first job, second job, small business.
Guilt over friends shows his progressive concern for others.
Hybrid finance-and-builder identity is strong and consistent.

steps.text: Take a first job that involves automating finance checks
Keep the freelance clients on evenings
Study data and compliance basics to be the person who checks the machine
Put a monthly amount into an index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a decade of runway and we should use it to build a fair system. Employers and governments need to commit now. I'd also say to my friends: start playing with the tools today, because you only learn by doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel pretty relaxed. I'd have time for a career, maybe a flat, maybe a small company of my own. But a decade can slip by while we argue, and I'd hate it if nothing happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a first job and a proper qualification. I'd keep freelancing and try to turn it into a small firm by 26. Mostly I'd save for a deposit and learn enough about what's coming to be ready for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a few nerves. It's the one where I think I can make my own luck, and that's a nice feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What might ten years change in how you plan your life?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd plan a flat, a partner someday, maybe kids at some point. With two years I couldn't. With ten, it's a real option.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a friend who is more worried?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say do three things: use the tools for a week and see, join a group of people in the same boat, and ask your manager what they're planning. It's not magic, it's practice. Being worried is okay, but being passive is not, so I'd tell my friends to try the tools for a week.

say: I'd say a decade is **runway**, so employers and governments should commit now.
I'd tell friends to start **playing with the tools** today.
think: I'd feel pretty **relaxed**, with time for a career, a flat and perhaps a small company.
I'd hate it if a decade slipped by while we **argued**.
do: Get a **first job** and a proper qualification.
Turn freelancing into a **small firm** by 26.
Save for a **deposit** and keep learning what's coming.
feel: **Calm** with a few nerves, feeling I can make my own luck.
S4.quote: Being worried is okay, but being passive is not, so I'd tell my friends to try the tools for a week.
fieldNote: Ivan is the most **settled** here: the decade lets him plan a flat, a firm and a family.
He still ties his comfort to fairness and to bringing friends along.
Advice to friends is practical: try tools, join a group, ask managers.

steps.text: Take a first accounting job and start a professional qualification
Grow freelancing into a small firm by 26

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most, mostly for everyone else. I can use the tools, but the banks, the councils and my parents' generation have no time to catch up. What would help is real public support: an income floor, retraining that's actually paid, and rules that stop firms dumping a whole department at once.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not scared of the tech. I'm annoyed at who gets the benefit. If a tool saves a firm a million, I want some of that to come back to the people who lost the hours.

headlineQuote: I'm not scared of the tech. I'm annoyed at who gets the benefit.
portrait: **Ivan** is a 23-year-old accounting graduate, top of his class, living with his parents and grandmother.
He uses **AI tools every day**, does freelance bookkeeping for two small shops, and builds spreadsheet automations for fun.
He is progressive, leaning on **unions and regulation**, and blames firms for hoarding the savings.
He moves first in every scenario, with **side income** and skills, while still pushing for fair rules.
His mood rises with speed, from uneasy to anxious only in the 2-year world.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture**, mainly for people with no time to catch up, like his parents.
whatWouldHelp: Rules that stop firms removing **whole departments** at once, and a share of savings returned to affected workers.
